settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: If the underlying stream returns -1 for a zero-length read, or if the request body ends, makeAvailable throws MalformedStreamException (line 1003) instead of spinning, terminating the parse.

The parser is normally wrapped in a size-limited stream (sizeMax is available and checked by FileItemIteratorImpl in the ranges not fully read), which can cap total bytes consumed even when the loop spins.
InputStream.read(byte[],int,int) implementations are permitted but not required to return 0 for len==0; many buffered streams do not.
candidates.description: MultipartStream constructs its fixed working buffer from bufSize and sets keepRegion from the boundary length, without requiring the buffer to be at least as large as the boundary: `this.buffer = new byte[bufSize]; ... this.boundaryLength = boundary.length + BOUNDARY_PREFIX.length; this.keepRegion = this.boundary.length;` (MultipartStream.java:329-336). The boundary is taken verbatim from the client-supplied Content-type header (FileUploadBase.getBoundary, lines 419-435, which lower-cases parameter names, reads `boundary`, and byte-encodes it with no length limit; FileItemIteratorImpl passes it to the MultipartStream constructor). The delimiter search can only find a boundary that lies fully inside the buffer: findSeparator computes `maxpos = tail - boundaryLength` and immediately returns -1 when maxpos < head (MultipartStream.java:697-718). So with boundaryLength larger than bufSize, no separator is ever found. In ItemInputStream.makeAvailable (MultipartStream.java:983-1017) the code moves `pad` bytes, sets `tail = pad`, and loops `int bytesRead = input.read(buffer, tail, bufSize - tail);` with no cap on iterations and no check for a zero-length read. When the buffer fills up, `bufSize - tail` becomes 0 and `tail += bytesRead` adds nothing, findSeparator again returns -1, and available() returns `tail - head - pad` (MultipartStream.java:846-851) which is 0, so the `if (av > 0 || pos != -1)` exit is not taken. A zero-length InputStream.read is permitted to return 0 indefinitely, so the loop can keep executing without consuming stream data or advancing the buffer, i.e. CPU consumption while parsing. I could not confirm in the read source that a concrete transport (e.g. a servlet request stream) returns 0 for a zero-length read rather than -1, nor that the surrounding FileItemIteratorImpl rejects an over-long boundary, so exploitability is unverified. The observation consistent with the code is that the guard which forces a buffer big enough for the boundary is missing.
missing_evidence: The body of MultipartStream.readBodyData/Streams.copy callers and the full FileItemIteratorImpl (FileUploadBase.java:550+ was not read) to confirm the boundary and buffer sizes actually used and whether any boundary-length validation is applied.
Whether the servlet/portlet input stream used in deployment returns 0 vs -1 for a zero-length read.
Whether an upstream layer (server/proxy) enforces a maximum Content-type/header length that would prevent an over-long boundary.
preconditions: Application invokes the package's multipart parsing (e.g. parseRequest/getItemIterator) on untrusted request data.

Attacker controls the multipart Content-type header and can supply a boundary token longer than the parser buffer size (DEFAULT_BUFSIZE = 4096 in FileUploadBase, MultipartStream DEFAULT_BUFSIZE = 4096, line 184).
The request body/stream backing the parse is such that a zero-length read returns 0 rather than -1 (common for unbuffered/blocking servlet or socket streams); not verifiable from the read source.
candidates.title: MultipartStream refill loop can spin without consuming input when the attacker-controlled boundary exceeds the internal buffer size

counter_evidence: sizeMax (FileUploadBase.java:157-161, 205-221) can bound total request size if configured; it is unlimited by default only.
'Accumulating a list of parsed items' is the documented, intended API behavior of parseRequest, so this is a design-level exhaustion concern rather than a coding defect.
Content-length-based pre-checks inside FileItemIteratorImpl (lines beyond 550, not read) may reject oversized requests before parsing.
candidates.description: In the read source, FileUploadBase.parseRequest builds a List of FileItem objects and iterates the parsed stream without any maximum-part (or maximum-file) count: `List<FileItem> items = new ArrayList<FileItem>(); ... while (iter.hasNext()) { final FileItemStream item = iter.next(); ... FileItem fileItem = fac.createItem(...); items.add(fileItem); ... }` (FileUploadBase.java:331-345). The only visible size-related controls are the deprecated MAX_HEADER_SIZE constant (1024, line 152-153) and the fields `sizeMax`/`fileSizeMax`, both documented as defaulting to -1 meaning no limit (lines 157-167), with setters that do not derive an item count. parseParameterMap (lines 389-406) then maps every parsed item into the returned structure. Consequently a request containing a very large number of small multipart parts can cause the parser to create and retain unbounded per-part state (a FileItem plus, for disk-backed items, temporary-file bookkeeping) for the duration of the parse, i.e. resource consumption proportional to the part count. No FileCountLimitExceededException-style type or configurable maximum-part field exists among the imported symbols (FileUpload.java import block, lines 21-40), although the read range is limited to the first 549 lines of FileUploadBase so an implementation further down cannot be fully excluded. Reachability of a real exhaustion depends on request size limits enforced by the application/container; this is reported as an unverified candidate.
missing_evidence: Full body of FileUploadBase.FileItemIteratorImpl (lines 550+) to see whether any part-count or item-count guard exists.
Whether the library's packaging or documentation imposes an item-count limit in this snapshot.
How the calling application configures sizeMax and whether the container limits the number of multipart parts.
preconditions: Application calls parseRequest/parseParameterMap on attacker-controlled multipart data.
The container or application does not impose a separate cap on total request size or on the number of parts.
Each part is small enough to pass any configured sizeMax/fileSizeMax while the count is large.
candidates.title: No limit on the number of multipart parts accumulated during parseRequest
